newsitem.title: UK: 900-year UK tradition of hunting fallow deer ends.
newsitem.headline: 900-year UK tradition of hunting fallow deer ends.

text.p: A British tradition dating back more than 900 years has ended with the closure of the last hunt for fallow deer.

The New Forest Buckhounds said on Tuesday it would not hunt fallow deer in southern England's New Forest this season, starting August 1. The hunt chairman said it was unlikely buckhounds would hunt again.
The main reason given was that the New Forest, a popular tourist destination, was now too crowded.
But a recently launched inquiry into hunting by the Forestry Commission meant the Buckhounds may well have been refused a licence for hunting on New Forest land owned by the commission.

Red and roe deer are still hunted in Britain. Deer-hunting has come under increasing pressure from animal rights activists. They have called on the Forestry Commission to suspend the buckhounds' licence following allegations of cruelty towards the deer.
The Buckhounds were founded in 1885, but hunting fallow deer has been a part of New Forest life since William the Conqueror designated the forest a royal hunting ground in 1079.

Despite animal rights concerns, British media said on Tuesday the Labour government was preparing to kill a proposed bill banning any fox and deer-hunting by not allowing it sufficient time to pass through parliament.

On July 10, 100,000 people crowded into London's Hyde Park to protest against the bill, launched by a Labour member of parliament. Political sources said such opposition appeared to have swayed the governnment.
